Appendix A Implementation Details of the Symbolic Perception Interface

This appendix details the technical implementation of the symbolic perception pipeline described in Section 3.2. The objective is to transform raw RGB-D observations OtO_{t} into a structured symbolic snapshot E​n​vtEnv_{t} efficiently.

A.1 Vocabulary-Guided 2D Attention Focusing

To avoid computationally expensive dense reconstruction of irrelevant background, we leverage the VLM to filter the scene in the 2D domain first.

a. Task-Relevant Category Generation:

Given the task description 𝒯\mathcal{T} and RGB image ItI_{t}, the VLM infers a list of relevant object categories 𝒞t​a​s​k\mathcal{C}_{task}:

𝒞t​a​s​k={c1,c2,…}=VLMi​n​f​e​r​e​n​c​e​(It,𝒯)\mathcal{C}_{task}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\dots\}=\text{VLM}_{inference}(I_{t},\mathcal{T}) (18)

Example: For 𝒯=\mathcal{T}= "Fetch the drink", 𝒞t​a​s​k→\mathcal{C}_{task}\rightarrow [’bottle’, ’can’, ’cup’, ’table’].

b. Open-Vocabulary Segmentation:

This list 𝒞t​a​s​k\mathcal{C}_{task} serves as the text prompt for an open-vocabulary segmentation model (specifically, we use “Mask2Former” trained on cityscapes/COCO). The model outputs a set of binary masks ℳ\mathcal{M}:

ℳ⁡(u,v)={(ci,IDi)∣SegModel​(It,𝒞t​a​s​k)}\mathcal{M}(u,v)=\{(c_{i},\text{ID}_{i})\mid\text{SegModel}(I_{t},\mathcal{C}_{task})\} (19)

Pixels not belonging to 𝒞t​a​s​k\mathcal{C}_{task} are masked out (n​u​l​lnull), significantly reducing the data volume for downstream 3D processing.

A.2 Sparse 3D Lifting and Coordinate Transformation

We establish a precise mapping from selected 2D pixels to the robot’s 3D workspace.

a. Depth Back-Projection:

For a valid pixel (u,v)(u,v) with depth d=Dt​(u,v)d=D_{t}(u,v), we project it to the camera coordinate frame pcp_{c}:

pc=d⋅𝐊−1​[u,v,1]⊤p_{c}=d\cdot\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,v,1]^{\top} (20)

where 𝐊\mathbf{K} is the camera intrinsic matrix.

b. Kinematic Transformation:

The point is then transformed to the robot base frame pbp_{b} using the kinematic chain:

pb=𝐓eb⋅𝐓ce⋅pcp_{b}={{}^{b}\mathbf{T}_{e}}\cdot{{}^{e}\mathbf{T}_{c}}\cdot p_{c} (21)

where 𝐓eb{{}^{b}\mathbf{T}_{e}} is the end-effector pose (from forward kinematics) and 𝐓ce{{}^{e}\mathbf{T}_{c}} is the hand-eye calibration matrix.

c. Ray-Casting Correspondence:

To robustly associate semantic masks with noisy depth data, we employ a ray-casting check. A ray 𝐫⁡(t)\mathbf{r}(t) originating from the optical center passes through pixel (u,v)(u,v) into the point cloud PbP_{b}. A point p∈Pbp\in P_{b} is assigned the label of pixel (u,v)(u,v) if and only if it lies within a distance threshold ϵ\epsilon of the ray:

‖𝐫⁡(t)×(p−𝐜)‖‖𝐫⁡(t)‖<ϵ\frac{\|\mathbf{r}(t)\times(p-\mathbf{c})\|}{\|\mathbf{r}(t)\|}<\epsilon (22)

This generates a sparse set of labeled 3D points: M​a​pt={(pbk,labelk,IDk)}Map_{t}=\{(p_{b}^{k},\text{label}_{k},\text{ID}_{k})\}.

A.3 Distance-Aware Multi-Resolution Quantization

We partition the workspace into concentric zones based on the robot’s physical reach capabilities.

a. Threshold Definition:
  • 1.

    rn​e​a​rr_{near} (e.g., 0.8m): The maximum reach of the robotic arm without base movement.

  • 2.

    rf​a​rr_{far} (e.g., 2.0m): The trusted sensing range for reliable object identification.

b. Quantization Logic:

Based on the centroid distance di=‖p¯i‖d_{i}=\|\bar{p}_{i}\|, the object’s geometry g​e​o​migeom_{i} is constructed as:

  • 1.

    Near Zone (di<rn​e​a​rd_{i}<r_{near}): We retain the raw point cloud 𝒫​𝒞i\mathcal{PC}_{i}. This supports high-fidelity ICP registration for grasping.

  • 2.

    Mid Zone (rn​e​a​r≤di<rf​a​rr_{near}\leq d_{i}<r_{far}): We discretize points into a Voxel Grid 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} (voxel size = 2cm). This preserves topology while compressing data for collision checking.

  • 3.

    Far Zone (di≥rf​a​rd_{i}\geq r_{far}): We abstract the object as a “Directed Billboard” ℬi=⟨Ic​r​o​p,v→v​i​e​w,𝐩c​e​n⟩\mathcal{B}_{i}=\langle I_{crop},\vec{v}_{view},\mathbf{p}_{cen}\rangle, where Ic​r​o​pI_{crop} is the RGB crop, v→v​i​e​w\vec{v}_{view} is the viewing vector, and 𝐩c​e​n\mathbf{p}_{cen} is the centroid. This acts as a visual proxy for situational awareness with minimal memory cost.

A.4 Final Symbolic Object Encapsulation

Finally, we aggregate the fragmented mappings into coherent object instances. For each unique instance ID detected in the mask set, we gather its geometric primitives and query the VLM for a descriptive summary. The final observation snapshot E​n​vtEnv_{t} is a set of tuples, where each object o​b​jitobj_{i}^{t} is defined as:

o​b​jit=⟨idi,labeli,g​e​o​mit,desci⟩obj_{i}^{t}=\langle\text{id}_{i},\text{label}_{i},geom_{i}^{t},\text{desc}_{i}\rangle (23)
  • 1.

    idi\text{id}_{i}: Unique instance identifier (e.g., "blue_block_1").

  • 2.

    labeli\text{label}_{i}: Semantic category from VLM (e.g., "block").

  • 3.

    g​e​o​mitgeom_{i}^{t}: The heterogeneous geometric representation derived in A.3.

  • 4.

    desci\text{desc}_{i}: A VLM-generated attribute description (e.g., "A metallic cube, possibly heavy").

A.5 Perception Pipeline Triggering Policy

The perception-to-memory pipeline (Section 3.2) does not run at a fixed frame rate. Instead, we employ an event-driven triggering policy to balance computational cost and state freshness.

A.5.1 Trigger Events

The full perception pipeline is invoked upon:

  1. 1.

    Action Boundary: Before and after each skill execution (e.g., pre-grasp, post-place).

  2. 2.

    Zone Transition: When the robot enters a new 𝒢z​o​n​e\mathcal{G}_{zone} region.

  3. 3.

    Anomaly Detection: When F/T feedback or motion tracking indicates unexpected events.

  4. 4.

    Explicit Query: When the VLM requests updated state for a specific object.

  5. 5.

    Timeout: If no trigger occurs for Tm​a​x=10T_{max}=10 seconds (background refresh).

A.5.2 Handling Drift During Non-Observation Periods

Between perception events, object states in 𝒮o​b​j\mathcal{S}_{obj} are not updated. We address potential drift through:

a. Conservative Covariance Inflation:

For each object oio_{i} not observed in the current cycle, we inflate its position uncertainty by a fixed process noise:

𝚺t​(oi)←𝚺t−1​(oi)+𝐐d​r​i​f​t\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}(o_{i})\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t-1}(o_{i})+\mathbf{Q}_{drift} (24)

where 𝐐d​r​i​f​t=diag​(0.001,0.001,0.001)​m2\mathbf{Q}_{drift}=\text{diag}(0.001,0.001,0.001)\,\text{m}^{2} represents per-cycle drift uncertainty (approximately 3 cm standard deviation per axis). This accumulation signals to the planner that unobserved objects have increased positional uncertainty.

b. Pre-Action Verification:

Before any manipulation action targeting object oio_{i}, the system mandatorily triggers a perception update for oio_{i}, regardless of recency. This ensures no action is executed based on stale beliefs.

c. Static Object Assumption:

For objects tagged as “static” in 𝒢\mathcal{G} (e.g., fixtures, tables), we assume zero drift and skip re-observation unless explicitly invalidated.

A.5.3 Complexity Implications

The event-driven policy means the per-cycle costs in E are amortized, not per-frame. In our experiments:

  • 1.

    Task 1 (Assembly): ∼\sim15 perception events over ∼\sim120 seconds (≈0.125\approx 0.125 Hz effective rate)

  • 2.

    Task 2 (Exploration): ∼\sim240 perception events over ∼\sim600 seconds (≈0.4\approx 0.4 Hz effective rate)

  • 3.

    Task 3 (Recovery): Variable, with bursts during failure diagnosis

This is significantly lower than continuous SLAM-style updates, validating the efficiency claims.

Appendix B Algorithmic Details for DEWM Dynamics and Maintenance

This appendix provides the specific hyperparameters, noise models, and prompt templates required to reproduce the DEWM dynamics.

B.1 Data Association and Similarity Scoring

This section specifies the association cost, gating rules, and VLM prompt templates used to match observations ok∈E​n​vto_{k}\in Env_{t} to memory entries si∈𝒮o​b​js_{i}\in\mathcal{S}_{obj} in the Hungarian assignment.

B.1.1 Association Cost and Weights

We construct a hybrid cost matrix:

Ck​i=λi​o​u⋅(1−IoU​(ok,si))+λs​e​m⋅(1−sim​(ok,si)),λi​o​u+λs​e​m=1.C_{ki}=\lambda_{iou}\cdot(1-\text{IoU}(o_{k},s_{i}))+\lambda_{sem}\cdot(1-\text{sim}(o_{k},s_{i})),\quad\lambda_{iou}+\lambda_{sem}=1. (25)

Unless otherwise stated, we set (λi​o​u,λs​e​m)=(0.7,0.3)(\lambda_{iou},\lambda_{sem})=(0.7,0.3), prioritizing geometric consistency while allowing semantic cues to resolve visually similar instances.

B.1.2 IoU Definition (3D/2D Fallback)

For each observation–memory pair, we compute IoU over 3D oriented bounding volumes when depth is reliable. If depth is unreliable (e.g., reflective surfaces or missing depth), we fall back to 2D mask IoU in the image plane using the most recent view:

IoU​(ok,si)={Vol​(ℬok∩ℬsi)Vol​(ℬok∪ℬsi),3D OBBs availableArea​(ℳok∩ℳsi)Area​(ℳok∪ℳsi),2D fallback\text{IoU}(o_{k},s_{i})=\begin{cases}\frac{\text{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{o_{k}}\cap\mathcal{B}_{s_{i}})}{\text{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{o_{k}}\cup\mathcal{B}_{s_{i}})},&\text{3D OBBs available}\\ \frac{\text{Area}(\mathcal{M}_{o_{k}}\cap\mathcal{M}_{s_{i}})}{\text{Area}(\mathcal{M}_{o_{k}}\cup\mathcal{M}_{s_{i}})},&\text{2D fallback}\end{cases} (26)

where ℬ\mathcal{B} denotes an oriented bounding volume and ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes a 2D segmentation mask.

B.1.3 Semantic Similarity Prompt and Parsing

The semantic similarity sim​(ok,si)∈[0,1]\text{sim}(o_{k},s_{i})\in[0,1] is queried from the VLM when geometric cues alone are ambiguous (e.g., multiple nearby candidates or visually similar parts). The inputs {loc} are 3D Euclidean coordinates relative to the robot base, and {feat} are short attribute strings extracted from perception.

We use greedy decoding with temperature 00 and parse the first numeric token in the VLM output as sim​(ok,si)\text{sim}(o_{k},s_{i}). If parsing fails, we set sim=0\text{sim}=0 as a conservative default. We use τs​i​m=0.5\tau_{sim}=0.5 as the neutral decision boundary.

B.1.4 Hungarian Assignment and Match Gating

Given Ck​iC_{ki}, we solve a one-to-one assignment using the Hungarian algorithm. A proposed match (ok,si)(o_{k},s_{i}) is accepted only if it passes a match-quality gate:

Ck​i≤τm​a​t​c​h.C_{ki}\leq\tau_{match}. (27)

Unless otherwise stated, we set τm​a​t​c​h=0.55\tau_{match}=0.55. This gate rejects low-confidence matches and prevents identity switches in cluttered scenes.

B.1.5 Confirmation Window for Unmatched Observations

If oko_{k} is not matched to any active entry (or all candidate matches violate τm​a​t​c​h\tau_{match}), it enters a confirmation window and is tracked tentatively for nc​o​n​f​i​r​mn_{confirm} consecutive observations before being promoted to a new active entity. We set nc​o​n​f​i​r​m=2n_{confirm}=2 by default. Tentative tracks that are not re-observed within the window are discarded, suppressing one-off false detections and preventing ghost artifacts.

B.2 Adaptive Fusion and VLM Gain Modulation

This section provides the implementation details for the VLM-modulated Gaussian envelope fusion described in Section 3.2.3.

B.2.1 Quantifying Observation Uncertainty (𝚺o​b​s\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{obs})

The observation covariance 𝚺o​b​s\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{obs} in Equations (7)–(8) is computed based on the geometric abstraction available at time tt:

  • 1.

    Near-Field (Point Cloud):

    𝚺o​b​s=1N−1​∑i=1N(𝐩i−𝝁o​b​s)​(𝐩i−𝝁o​b​s)⊤+ϵ​𝐈,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{obs}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbf{p}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{obs})(\mathbf{p}_{i}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{obs})^{\top}+\epsilon\mathbf{I}, (28)

    where NN is the point count and ϵ=10−6​m2\epsilon=10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2} prevents singularities.

  • 2.

    Mid/Far-Field (Bounding Volume):

    𝚺o​b​s=diag​(σx2,σy2,σz2),\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{obs}=\text{diag}(\sigma_{x}^{2},\sigma_{y}^{2},\sigma_{z}^{2}), (29)

    with default (σx,σy,σz)=(0.01,0.01,0.02)(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z})=(0.01,0.01,0.02) meters.

B.3 Scale-Aware Robust ICP Solver Details

To handle scale discrepancies (e.g., between canonical CAD models and real-world instances) and sensor noise, we solve the joint optimization problem:

(𝐓^,s^)=arg⁡min⁡∑i=1N𝐑,𝐭,s⁡ρδ​(‖s⁡(𝐑​pi+𝐭)−qi‖2)(\hat{\mathbf{T}},\hat{s})=\arg\min_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t},s}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\rho_{\delta}\left(\|s(\mathbf{R}p_{i}+\mathbf{t})-q_{i}\|^{2}\right) (30)

where pi∈𝒫∗p_{i}\in\mathcal{P}^{*} are source model points and qiq_{i} are corresponding target points.

a. Robust Cost Function:

We use the Huber loss ρδ​(⋅)\rho_{\delta}(\cdot) to mitigate the effect of outliers (e.g., segmentation artifacts):

ρδ​(r)={12​r2for ​|r|≤δδ⁡(|r|−12​δ)otherwise\rho_{\delta}(r)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}r^{2}&\text{for }|r|\leq\delta\\ \delta(|r|-\frac{1}{2}\delta)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (31)

We adaptively set δ=2.5⋅median​(r)\delta=2.5\cdot\text{median}(r) at each iteration.

b. Closed-Form Update Steps:

While the joint optimization is non-convex, we decouple it into two convex sub-problems solved iteratively.At each iteration, we compute weights from the Huber loss:

wi=ρδ′​(ri)ri,ri=‖s⁡(𝐑​pi+𝐭)−qi‖w_{i}=\frac{\rho^{\prime}_{\delta}(r_{i})}{r_{i}},\quad r_{i}=\|s(\mathbf{R}p_{i}+\mathbf{t})-q_{i}\| (32)

where ρδ′\rho^{\prime}_{\delta} is the derivative of the Huber function (ρδ′​(r)=min⁡(1,δ/|r|)⋅sign​(r)\rho^{\prime}_{\delta}(r)=\min(1,\delta/|r|)\cdot\text{sign}(r)).

  • 1.

    Pose Update (𝐑,𝐭\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t}): Using the weighted centroids p¯=∑wi​pi∑wi\bar{p}=\frac{\sum w_{i}p_{i}}{\sum w_{i}} and q¯=∑wi​qi∑wi\bar{q}=\frac{\sum w_{i}q_{i}}{\sum w_{i}}, we compute the cross-covariance matrix 𝐇=∑iwi​(pi−p¯)​(qi−q¯)⊤\mathbf{H}=\sum_{i}w_{i}(p_{i}-\bar{p})(q_{i}-\bar{q})^{\top}. The rotation is derived via SVD:

    𝐔​𝚲​𝐕⊤=SVD​(𝐇),𝐑=𝐕𝐔⊤\mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\top}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{H}),\quad\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{\top} (33)

    Check: If det(𝐑)<0\det(\mathbf{R})<0, we correct 𝐕\mathbf{V} by multiplying its last column by -1 to ensure a valid rotation.

  • 2.

    Scale Update (ss): With 𝐑,𝐭\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t} fixed, the optimal scale is analytically derived:

    s=∑iwi​(qi−q¯)⊤​𝐑​(pi−p¯)∑iwi​‖pi−p¯‖2s=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}(q_{i}-\bar{q})^{\top}\mathbf{R}(p_{i}-\bar{p})}{\sum_{i}w_{i}\|p_{i}-\bar{p}\|^{2}} (34)

B.4 Background Map Maintenance Implementation

The background model 𝒮b​g\mathcal{S}_{bg} employs a hybrid volumetric-visual representation.

a. Probabilistic Volumetric Fusion:

For voxel occupancy O⁡(n)O(n), we use the standard log-odds notation L⁡(n)=log⁡P⁡(O⁡(n))1−P⁡(O⁡(n))L(n)=\log\frac{P(O(n))}{1-P(O(n))}. The update rule for measurement ztz_{t} is:

L(n|z1:t)=clamp(L(n|z1:t−1)+L(n|zt),lm​i​n,lm​a​x)L(n|z_{1:t})=\text{clamp}\left(L(n|z_{1:t-1})+L(n|z_{t}),l_{min},l_{max}\right) (35)

where lm​i​n=−2,lm​a​x=3.5l_{min}=-2,l_{max}=3.5 prevent over-confidence.

Simultaneously, we maintain a semantic distribution P(Ck|z1:t)P(C_{k}|z_{1:t}) over classes Ck∈{wall, table, floor, …}C_{k}\in\{\text{wall, table, floor, ...}\} using a recursive Bayesian update:

P(Ck|z1:t)=ηP(zt|Ck)P(Ck|z1:t−1)P(C_{k}|z_{1:t})=\eta\,P(z_{t}|C_{k})\,P(C_{k}|z_{1:t-1}) (36)

where η=(∑k′P(zt|Ck′)P(Ck′|z1:t−1))−1\eta=\left(\sum_{k^{\prime}}P(z_{t}|C_{k^{\prime}})P(C_{k^{\prime}}|z_{1:t-1})\right)^{-1} ensures normalization.

b. Directed Billboard Management:

For ray endpoints exceeding rf​a​rr_{far}, we generate a visual proxy.

  • 1.

    Storage: A billboard ℬk=⟨Ic​r​o​p,v→v​i​e​w,𝐩c​e​n⟩\mathcal{B}_{k}=\langle I_{crop},\vec{v}_{view},\mathbf{p}_{cen}\rangle stores the RGB appearance Ic​r​o​pI_{crop} and the viewing direction v→c​a​m\vec{v}_{cam}.

  • 2.

    Retrieval Metric: When the planner queries a frontier direction v→q​u​e​r​y\vec{v}_{query}, we retrieve the most relevant billboard k∗k^{*} maximizing cosine similarity:

    k∗=arg⁡maxk⁡(v→q​u​e​r​y⋅v→v​i​e​wk‖v→q​u​e​r​y‖​‖v→v​i​e​wk‖)k^{*}=\arg\max_{k}\left(\frac{\vec{v}_{query}\cdot\vec{v}_{view}^{k}}{\|\vec{v}_{query}\|\|\vec{v}_{view}^{k}\|}\right) (37)

    This simple metric effectively handles the view-dependent nature of open boundaries (e.g., looking "out" a window vs. looking "at" a wall).

B.5 Statistical Basis for Geometric Verification

The verification module treats relation proposals as statistical hypothesis tests. We assume the position estimates of objects follow multivariate normal distributions 𝒩⁡(𝝁,𝚺)\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}).

a. Containment Test (A⊃BA\supset B):

The condition verifies if the bulk of BB’s probability mass lies within the high-likelihood region of AA. We compute the Mahalanobis distance of BB’s centroid relative to AA’s distribution:

Dc​o​n​t​a​i​n2=(𝝁B−𝝁A)⊤​𝚺A−1​(𝝁B−𝝁A)D^{2}_{contain}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}) (38)

Note that only 𝚺A\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A} is used in the metric because the constraint is defined by the boundary of AA.

b. Contact Test (A​ touches ​BA\text{ touches }B):

This tests the hypothesis that the two distributions overlap significantly. The uncertainty of the relative difference vector Δ​𝐱=𝐱B−𝐱A\Delta\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_{B}-\mathbf{x}_{A} is given by the convolution of variances (sum of covariance matrices):

Dc​o​n​t​a​c​t2=(𝝁B−𝝁A)⊤​(𝚺A+𝚺B)−1​(𝝁B−𝝁A)D^{2}_{contact}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{A}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{B})^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}) (39)
c. Threshold Selection (χt​h​r​e​s​h2\chi^{2}_{thresh}):

The squared Mahalanobis distance follows a Chi-square distribution with kk degrees of freedom. Since we evaluate spatial relations in 3D translational space (x,y,zx,y,z), we set k=3k=3. For a strict 95% confidence level (i.e., we are 95% sure the relation holds), we consult the χ2\chi^{2} table:

P⁡(X≤χt​h​r​e​s​h2|k=3)=0.95⟹χt​h​r​e​s​h2≈7.815P(X\leq\chi^{2}_{thresh}|k=3)=0.95\implies\chi^{2}_{thresh}\approx 7.815 (40)

Any relation with a distance score D2>7.815D^{2}>7.815 is rejected as a statistical anomaly or noise.

B.6 Long-Term Memory Lifecycle Management

To ensure robustness in long-horizon operations, the “Memory Curation” is not merely a deletion process but a full Entity Lifecycle Management system. We define three states for every memory entity: Active, Uncertain, and Archived.

a. State Transitions and Decay Dynamics:

When the robot performs a perception scan in Zone ZkZ_{k}, the confidence ctc_{t} of an unobserved entity viv_{i} follows an exponential decay model, representing the increasing probability that the object has been moved or removed:

ct​(vi)=ct−1​(vi)⋅λd​e​c​a​yc_{t}(v_{i})=c_{t-1}(v_{i})\cdot\lambda_{decay} (41)

Entities transition states based on thresholds:

  • 1.

    Active →\to Uncertain: When ct<τu​n​c​e​r​t​a​i​nc_{t}<\tau_{uncertain} (set to 0.6). The planner adds a "Verify" sub-task before interacting.

  • 2.

    Uncertain →\to Archived: When ct<τa​r​c​h​i​v​ec_{t}<\tau_{archive} (set to 0.1). The entity is removed from the spatial index tree (KD-Tree) to optimize query speed but retained in cold storage (Disk).

b. Restoration of Archived Entities (The "Zombie" Problem):

A critical feature is the ability to recover from false negatives. If a new observation on​e​wo_{new} appears but fails to match any Active entity, the system queries the Archived database. If a match is found (using the logic in B.1), the entity is restored to Active state with ctc_{t} reset to 1.0, preserving its historical semantic attributes (e.g., "fragile").

c. Curation Algorithm:

The complete lifecycle maintenance logic is detailed in Algorithm 3.

Parameter Rationale: We select λd​e​c​a​y=0.95\lambda_{decay}=0.95. This implies a "half-life" of approx 13 scans. The archiving threshold τa​r​c​h​i​v​e=0.1\tau_{archive}=0.1 requires ≈45\approx 45 consecutive misses, providing a robust buffer against transient occlusions common in collaborative construction.

B.7 Force-Torque Feedback Integration

While VLM-DEWM focuses on cognitive-level planning (not low-level impedance control), the system interfaces with the robot controller’s force-torque (F/T) signals to trigger state transitions in the C​SCS module. This section specifies the integration protocol.

a. Scope Clarification

We do not design force control laws. Instead, we treat F/T readings as binary event triggers that signal the success or failure of contact-rich actions to the cognitive layer. The underlying impedance/admittance control is handled by the robot’s native controller (Franka Control Interface in our experiments).

b. Threshold-Based Event Detection

For each contact-rich action type, we define conservative thresholds based on the Franka Emika Panda’s specifications and empirical tuning:

c. Mapping to C​SCS State Transitions

The F/T events are mapped to C​SCS updates as follows:

  • 1.

    Grasp Failure (Fg<5F_{g}<5N after gripper close command):
    C​SCS remains at ⟨Idle,NULL⟩\langle\texttt{Idle},\texttt{NULL}\rangle; ERT’s 𝒜c​a​u​s​a​l\mathcal{A}_{causal} is invalidated.

  • 2.

    Collision Detected (|Fe​x​t|>15|F_{ext}|>15N during transport):
    Motion halts; C​SCS transitions to ⟨Interrupted,last_target⟩\langle\texttt{Interrupted},\text{last\_target}\rangle; triggers re-perception.

  • 3.

    Contact Confirmed (Fz>10F_{z}>10N sustained for 0.5s during place):
    C​SCS transitions from ⟨Placing,obj⟩\langle\texttt{Placing},\text{obj}\rangle to ⟨Idle,NULL⟩\langle\texttt{Idle},\texttt{NULL}\rangle; placement success logged.

d. Implementation Note

These thresholds are fixed in our experiments, calibrated once for the Franka+Robotiq platform. For deployment on different hardware, re-calibration is required. Adaptive thresholding based on object properties (e.g., fragile objects use lower FgF_{g} limits) is a direction for future work (Section 4.4.2).

Appendix C Implementation Details of Dynamic Context Engineering

This appendix details the subgraph extraction algorithm and prompt synthesis logic for the context engineering pipeline described in Section 3.3.2.

C.1 Task-Relevant Subgraph Extraction Algorithm

The “Information Bottleneck” principle in Section 3.3.2 is operationalized through a two-stage filtering algorithm, not learned compression. We prioritize interpretability and determinism over optimality.

C.1.1 Stage 1: Zone-Based Spatial Filtering

Given the current subtask s​stss_{t} and robot state C​StCS_{t}, we first identify the relevant zones:

𝒵r​e​l​e​v​a​n​t={Zc​u​r​r​e​n​t}∪{Z∈𝒢z​o​n​e∣Z mentioned in sst.goal}\mathcal{Z}_{relevant}=\{Z_{current}\}\cup\{Z\in\mathcal{G}_{zone}\mid Z\text{ mentioned in }ss_{t}.\text{goal}\} (42)

This exploits the hierarchical structure of 𝒢\mathcal{G} to immediately prune objects in distant, task-irrelevant areas.

Example: For s​st=ss_{t}= “Pick red_block from Zone_A”, we have 𝒵r​e​l​e​v​a​n​t={Zone_A}\mathcal{Z}_{relevant}=\{\text{Zone\_A}\}, ignoring all objects in Zone_B, Zone_C, etc.

C.1.2 Stage 2: Task-Driven Relevance Scoring

Within 𝒵r​e​l​e​v​a​n​t\mathcal{Z}_{relevant}, we compute a relevance score for each vertex vi∈𝒢o​b​jv_{i}\in\mathcal{G}_{obj}:

r⁡(vi)=w1⋅𝕀[vi∈sst.args]+w2⋅𝕀[∃e:(vi,vj)∧vj∈sst.args]+w3⋅sim(vi.cat,sst.keywords)\begin{split}r(v_{i})&=w_{1}\cdot\mathbb{I}[v_{i}\in ss_{t}.\text{args}]\\ &\quad+w_{2}\cdot\mathbb{I}[\exists e:(v_{i},v_{j})\land v_{j}\in ss_{t}.\text{args}]\\ &\quad+w_{3}\cdot\text{sim}(v_{i}.\text{cat},ss_{t}.\text{keywords})\end{split} (43)

where:

  • 1.

    w1=1.0w_{1}=1.0: Direct task arguments (e.g., the object to be picked)

  • 2.

    w2=0.5w_{2}=0.5: 1-hop neighbors of task arguments (e.g., the surface it’s on)

  • 3.

    w3=0.2w_{3}=0.2: Semantic similarity to task keywords (e.g., “container” for a packing task)

  • 4.

    sim​(⋅)\text{sim}(\cdot): Embedding cosine similarity (precomputed, not runtime VLM call)

C.1.3 Subgraph Construction

The extracted subgraph Gs​u​bG_{sub} is formed by selecting vertices that exceed a relevance threshold:

Vs​u​b\displaystyle V_{sub} ={vi∣r⁡(vi)>τr​e​l}∪{vr​o​b​o​t}\displaystyle=\{v_{i}\mid r(v_{i})>\tau_{rel}\}\cup\{v_{robot}\} (44)
Es​u​b\displaystyle E_{sub} ={ei​j∈ℰ∣vi∈Vs​u​b∧vj∈Vs​u​b}\displaystyle=\{e_{ij}\in\mathcal{E}\mid v_{i}\in V_{sub}\land v_{j}\in V_{sub}\} (45)

We set τr​e​l=0.3\tau_{rel}=0.3 empirically. This value was chosen to effectively prune irrelevant background objects (typically r<0.2r<0.2) while retaining indirect dependencies (e.g., support surfaces with r≈0.5r\approx 0.5). This filtering typically yields |Vs​u​b|≈3|V_{sub}|\approx 3–88 vertices for standard manipulation tasks.

C.1.4 Algorithm Pseudocode

C.1.5 Clarification on “Information Bottleneck”

We use the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle as a conceptual motivation, not a learned objective. Our rule-based extraction approximates the IB goal of minimizing I⁡(Z,Ω)I(Z;\Omega) (irrelevant info) while maximizing I⁡(Z,Y)I(Z;Y) (task-relevant info) through:

  • 1.

    Zone filtering ≈\approx spatial compression

  • 2.

    Relevance scoring ≈\approx task-conditional selection

A learned IB encoder (e.g., via variational methods) is left for future work.

C.6 Formal Definition of Semantic Discrepancy Operator (⊖\ominus)

The semantic discrepancy Δ=Ωt+1⊖𝒜c​a​u​s​a​l\Delta=\Omega_{t+1}\ominus\mathcal{A}_{causal} in Section 3.3.5 is computed via a rule-based state comparison, not probabilistic VLM inference. This ensures deterministic and auditable diagnosis.

a. Definition

Given the expected post-state 𝒜c​a​u​s​a​l=⟨C​Se​x​p,ℛe​x​p⟩\mathcal{A}_{causal}=\langle CS_{exp},\mathcal{R}_{exp}\rangle (where C​Se​x​pCS_{exp} is the expected constraint state and ℛe​x​p\mathcal{R}_{exp} is a set of expected relation changes) and the actual observed state Ωt+1\Omega_{t+1}, we define:

Δ=Ωt+1⊖𝒜c​a​u​s​a​l:=⟨ΔC​S,Δ𝒢,Δ𝒮⟩\Delta=\Omega_{t+1}\ominus\mathcal{A}_{causal}:=\langle\Delta_{CS},\Delta_{\mathcal{G}},\Delta_{\mathcal{S}}\rangle (46)
b. Component-wise Computation:

b.1. Constraint State Discrepancy (ΔC​S\Delta_{CS}): A direct symbolic comparison between expected and actual micro-topological states:

ΔC​S={NULLif ​C​St+1=C​Se​x​p(C​Se​x​p,C​St+1)otherwise\Delta_{CS}=\begin{cases}\texttt{NULL}&\text{if }CS_{t+1}=CS_{exp}\\ (CS_{exp},CS_{t+1})&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (47)

Example: If C​Se​x​p=⟨Holding,obj_1⟩CS_{exp}=\langle\texttt{Holding},\text{obj\_1}\rangle but C​St+1=⟨Idle,NULL⟩CS_{t+1}=\langle\texttt{Idle},\texttt{NULL}\rangle, then ΔC​S=(Holding→Idle)\Delta_{CS}=(\texttt{Holding}\to\texttt{Idle}), indicating a grasp failure.

b.2. Semantic Graph Discrepancy (Δ𝒢\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}): We perform a structural graph difference on the object-level semantic graph:

Δ𝒢+\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}^{+} =ℰt+1∖ℰe​x​p(unexpected new edges)\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{t+1}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{exp}\quad\text{(unexpected new edges)} (48)
Δ𝒢−\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}^{-} =ℰe​x​p∖ℰt+1(missing expected edges)\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{exp}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{t+1}\quad\text{(missing expected edges)} (49)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} denotes the edge set of 𝒢o​b​j\mathcal{G}_{obj}. This is implemented as a deterministic set operation on relation tuples.

Example: If the action was Place(A, B) with ℛe​x​p={+On​(A,B)}\mathcal{R}_{exp}=\{+\texttt{On}(A,B)\}, but post-observation shows On​(A,floor)\texttt{On}(A,\texttt{floor}), then:

  • 1.

    Δ𝒢−={On​(A,B)}\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}^{-}=\{\texttt{On}(A,B)\} (expected edge missing)

  • 2.

    Δ𝒢+={On​(A,floor)}\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}^{+}=\{\texttt{On}(A,\texttt{floor})\} (unexpected edge present)

b.3. Geometric Discrepancy (Δ𝒮\Delta_{\mathcal{S}}): For objects involved in the action, we compute the pose deviation:

Δ𝒮​(oi)=‖𝝁t+1​(oi)−𝝁e​x​p​(oi)‖2\Delta_{\mathcal{S}}(o_{i})=\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t+1}(o_{i})-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{exp}(o_{i})\|_{2} (50)

A significant deviation (>τg​e​o​_​d​r​i​f​t>\tau_{geo\_drift}, default 0.05m) flags potential unmodeled disturbances.

This rule-based approach ensures that the ⊖\ominus operator produces deterministic, explainable discrepancy reports, while the subsequent VLM call (C.5) is responsible only for recovery strategy synthesis—not diagnosis itself.

Appendix D Implementation Details of the ERT Validation Protocol

This appendix details the schema and verification logic for the External Reasoning Trace (ERT) described in Section 3.3.3.

D.1 ERT Schema Definition

The VLM output must strictly adhere to the schema defined in Table 10.

D.2 Multi-Layered Validation Logic

The GetValidERT() function enforces a three-stage check:

a. Syntactic Validation:

We use a JSON schema validator to ensure the output contains all required fields (Table 10) and that data types are correct (e.g., 0.0≤confidence≤1.00.0\leq\texttt{confidence}\leq 1.0).

b. Semantic Validation:

We extract all entity IDs from action_proposal and world_belief. The validator queries the DEWM to ensure existence:

∀i​d∈ℰe​r​t,(i​d∈𝒢o​b​j)∨(i​d∈𝒢z​o​n​e)\forall id\in\mathcal{E}_{ert},\quad(id\in\mathcal{G}_{obj})\lor(id\in\mathcal{G}_{zone}) (51)

This prevents hallucinations of non-existent objects.

c. Physical Consistency Validation:

We verify the world_belief against the geometric ground truth 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

  • 1.

    Verify On(A, B):

    1. (a)

      Support: Check if AA’s centroid 𝝁A\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A} projected onto the XY plane lies within BB’s XY-envelope.

    2. (b)

      Contact: Check if the vertical gap is minimal: |Zm​i​n​(A)−Zm​a​x​(B)|<ϵc​o​n​t​a​c​t|Z_{min}(A)-Z_{max}(B)|<\epsilon_{contact}.

  • 2.

    Verify Inside(A, B): Check if AA’s bounding box is fully contained within BB’s boundaries:

    (𝐦𝐢𝐧A≥𝐦𝐢𝐧B)∧(𝐦𝐚𝐱A≤𝐦𝐚𝐱B)(\mathbf{min}_{A}\geq\mathbf{min}_{B})\land(\mathbf{max}_{A}\leq\mathbf{max}_{B}) (52)
  • 3.

    Verify Near(A, B): Check Euclidean distance: ‖𝝁A−𝝁B‖<dn​e​a​r\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B}\|<d_{near}.

Appendix E Computational Complexity Analysis

This appendix analyzes the computational complexity of the VLM-DEWM framework. The overall cost comprises three main components: (1) perception and world model update, (2) dynamic context engineering, and (3) VLM inference and validation. We assume the DEWM maintains No​b​jN_{obj} object instances, and each perception snapshot E​n​vtEnv_{t} observes No​b​sN_{obs} objects.

E.1 Per-Cycle Update Cost

This is the foundational cost incurred in each cognitive cycle.

a. Symbolic Perception Interface

The VLM-driven semantic focusing requires one VLM call. Geometric processing (point cloud segmentation, projection, voxelization) scales as O⁡(Np​o​i​n​t​s)O(N_{points}) with the input point cloud size. Due to task-driven focusing, the actual processed point cloud is significantly smaller than the full scene.

b. Data Association

This is one of the main bottlenecks in the update process.

  • 1.

    Geometric Candidate Screening: A naive implementation comparing No​b​sN_{obs} observations against No​b​jN_{obj} memory entries has complexity O⁡(No​b​s⋅No​b​j)O(N_{obs}\cdot N_{obj}). In our implementation, by leveraging the Hierarchical Semantic Graph (HSG) for spatial indexing (first matching to Zone) and octree-based nearest neighbor search on the Spatial Network 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the average complexity is reduced to O⁡(No​b​s​log⁡No​b​j)O(N_{obs}\log N_{obj}).

  • 2.

    VLM Semantic Adjudication: For each observation, we select from kk geometric candidates (typically k≪No​b​jk\ll N_{obj}), requiring No​b​s⋅kN_{obs}\cdot k VLM scoring calls (optimizable via batching), or a single VLM call containing all candidates.

c. Geometric Layer Update (S-Update)

For each successfully associated object (at most No​b​sN_{obs}), the Gaussian envelope fusion (Equations 7–8) is O⁡(1)O(1). When high-precision pose estimation is required, the scale-aware ICP algorithm has complexity O⁡(I⋅Np​log⁡Np)O(I\cdot N_{p}\log N_{p}), where II is the number of iterations and NpN_{p} is the number of points in the object’s local point cloud.

d. Semantic Layer Update (G-Update)

VLM relation hypothesis generation requires one VLM call. The geometric verification step checks object-pair relations; in the worst case, this could involve O⁡(No​b​j2)O(N_{obj}^{2}) pairs, but in practice, the VLM typically proposes only a constant number of the most relevant relation hypotheses. Each hypothesis verification (e.g., Mahalanobis distance computation) is O⁡(1)O(1).

E.2 Context Engineering Cost

The goal of this process is to extract task-relevant information from the DEWM.

a. Subgraph Extraction

Thanks to the hierarchical structure of HSG, we first perform O⁡(1)O(1) indexing to identify the relevant Zone nodes. This restricts the search space from the global graph size |Vg​l​o​b​a​l||V_{global}| to the local zone size |Vz​o​n​e||V_{zone}| (where |Vz​o​n​e|≪|Vg​l​o​b​a​l||V_{zone}|\ll|V_{global}|). Consequently, the relevance scoring involves iterating only over |Vz​o​n​e||V_{zone}|, while the text serialization complexity scales with the much smaller final subgraph size O⁡(|Vs​u​b|+|Es​u​b|)O(|V_{sub}|+|E_{sub}|). Since |Vz​o​n​e||V_{zone}| is physically bounded (i.e., independent of the total facility scale), the overall context engineering overhead remains O⁡(1)O(1) relative to the global DEWM scale.

E.3 VLM-Guided Planning Cost

a. VLM Inference

VLM inference is the highest-latency component of the entire framework. Its complexity depends on the model architecture (typically Transformer) and input/output lengths. We can approximate it as f⁡(Lp​r​o​m​p​t,Lg​e​n)f(L_{prompt},L_{gen}), where Lp​r​o​m​p​tL_{prompt} is the token length of the context and prompt, and Lg​e​nL_{gen} is the token length of the generated ERT. A core objective of dynamic context engineering is to minimize Lp​r​o​m​p​tL_{prompt}.

b. ERT Validation
  • 1.

    Syntactic Validation: JSON schema validation scales linearly with ERT length, O⁡(Lg​e​n)O(L_{gen}).

  • 2.

    Semantic Validation: Checking whether entities in the ERT exist in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. If 𝒢\mathcal{G}’s vertices are stored using a hash table, each lookup has average complexity O⁡(1)O(1).

  • 3.

    Physical Consistency Validation: Checking w​o​r​l​d​_​b​e​l​i​e​fworld\_belief against 𝒮\mathcal{S} typically involves O⁡(1)O(1) geometric computations.

E.4 Summary

The main computational bottlenecks are VLM inference latency and data association overhead in densely cluttered scenes. Our architectural design, particularly the Hierarchical Semantic Graph (HSG) and Dynamic Context Engineering, aims to significantly prune the search space through spatial and task context, thereby effectively controlling the growth of data association cost and VLM context length. This enables the system to maintain high operational efficiency even when facing long-term, complex tasks.
